comment.value:
This paper introduces a new approach for online experimental design for directed brain stimulation. It's a clear and well-specified problem, in a challenging domain; all reviewers were impressed by the strength of the validation, which includes exploring different model architectures, and also real-world lab experiments that demonstrate the approach actually working in a real-world scenario. There was a consensus to accept among all reviewers, though borderline for most.

The major concerns were around clarity and scope of the machine learning contributions; this has been well-discussed in the author rebuttal period. For the final version of the paper, it should incorporate aspects discussed here, including making connections to RL and PPO clearer, making it more accessible to machine learning researchers (e.g. by clarifying the representation of the brain state early on), and making clear the connections to MiSO in the background sections. In particular all the "clarity" issues from reviewer moJh should be addressed.

One reviewer had a more fundamental concern regarding the hardware limitations of the approach used here, but not strongly enough to discourage acceptance.

author_final_remarks.value:
We appreciate the reviews and discussions, which helped clarify the significance and novelty of our work. We will revise our manuscript accordingly.

Our contribution lies in the novel integration of diverse machine learning approaches to achieve higher accuracy in reaching specified neural activity states, thereby advancing neuromodulation technologies for both understanding the brain and treating brain disorders. Designing a framework that works reliably in neuroscience settings is non-trivial because it requires addressing domain-specific challenges such as inter-trial and inter-session neural variability (arising from shifting brain states over time, recording instabilities, and changes in neural circuits), limited numbers of neural recording samples, and the need to interface with neural recording and stimulation devices in real time. Each component of OMiSO was carefully chosen after extensive experimentation to meet these constraints.

Compared to the similar, previously proposed framework MiSO, our new framework OMiSO:
1. Incorporates brain state information prior to stimulation to achieve higher accuracy in reaching specified activity states
2. Uses an online model for sample-efficient online learning
3. Leverages this online model to extend the stimulation parameter space beyond what was feasible in MiSO

Our goals include advancing both clinical and neuroscience research applications. OMiSO was designed to be adaptable to both contexts by allowing the user to set suitable target brain states based on each application, as well as to define the appropriateness of a given stimulation pattern for achieving that state (Eq. 7). The generality of OMiSO also enables future extensions, including delivery of stimulation sequences over time, combination of electrical stimulation with different sensory stimuli, and generation of neural activity sequences by incorporating a dynamical model of the brain that predicts future neural activity.

Thank you to the reviewer for the constructive comments and careful reading. Our responses are in the text below:
> 1. The authors claim...

We appreciate the suggestion. Although we did not incorporate the location of the target dots as features, we agree that incorporating it could improve model prediction. More broadly, this direction opens up an interesting opportunity to combine electrical stimulation with, for example, visual stimuli to not only improve the prediction precision but also increase the diversity of achievable neural population activity states. The use of visual stimuli to induce diverse neural population activity states has been explored in recent work (e.g., Cowley et al., 2017; Bashivan et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2019), which demonstrated that optimization of visual stimuli can shape neural population activity. Incorporating such stimuli into our framework is an interesting direction for future research.
> 1. Equations (1-4) are...

The reviewer is right that there is no conceptual difference in the latent alignment procedure between MiSO and OMiSO. We will make this section more concise by citing MiSO paper.
> 2. It wasn’t clear...

This is a great point. We will add a sentence in Section 2.3 to explain the model and architecture we used for our validation. We will also add a similar sentence in Section 2.4 for the stimulus-response inverse model.
> 3. It wasn’t clear in the...

Yes, the reviewer’s understanding is correct. While $Z$ contains multiple timesteps of latent activity making it a matrix, $\mathbf{z}$ is a vector containing only one timestep of latent activity. In revision, we will clarify the difference between them when introducing the $Z$ matrix.
> 4. The authors mention...

Thank you for pointing this out. We will cite S6 instead of S4.
> 5. It wasn’t clear...

For each trial, our experimental system randomly selected which method to use. In Fig. 4D, each dot represents the _actual_ neural activity induced by the selected stimulation pattern by the selected method on a single trial. The circled dot in each panel indicates the average induced activity across trials for that method within an example session.
 
To generate Fig. 4E, for each session, we first computed the Euclidean distance between the target state and the induced neural activity for each trial (i.e., each dot in Fig. 4D), and then averaged these distances across trials separately for each method. For each method, we then computed the mean and standard deviation of these session-level averages across the 14 sessions.
> For L312, should...

Yes, they are p=0.05 and p=0.01. More specifically, they are p=0.048 and p=0.011.
> 6. L157: The number...

We will change the notation from $\\mathbb{R}$ to $\\mathbb{Z}$.
> 7. L195: What does...

The baseline b ensures the advantage can take both positive and negative values. Without it (i.e., b=0), the advantage (eq. 7) becomes always negative. This would cause the model parameter updates to consistently reduce the predicted suitability of all stimulation patterns, leading to unstable learning. With baseline b, the advantage $A_{c,k}$ becomes positive for stimulation patterns with smaller errors than b and negative for those with larger errors. This encourages increasing the probability of better-performing patterns and decreasing that of worse ones, helping the model converge more stably and quickly toward small-error stimulation patterns.
> 8. After doing...

We selected _l_ target latent dimensions satisfying two conditions: 1) they aligned well across multiple sessions, and 2) diverse latent activity states could be induced along these dimensions with uStim (S3, line 457). We made this choice because not all latent dimensions are equally suitable for reliable perturbation of neural activity. For example, some dimensions may be aligned poorly across sessions because they are not consistently present in every session, while others may not be directly modifiable by uStim.

If we set l=m=5, the optimization problem becomes more challenging because it may require optimizing over a larger parameter space (e.g., optimizing stimulation amplitude, in addition to stimulation locations) to find the stimulation pattern which can create a target state along all 5 dimensions. We expect OMiSO to still outperform MiSO in this scenario because OMiSO is designed to explore a larger parameter space to produce more diverse brain states and leverage brain state information to improve prediction accuracy.
 
If we set l=m=2, the alignment across sessions may deteriorate, leading to lower performance for both MiSO and OMiSO. 5 dimensions were identified as the optimal latent dimensionality that captures variance shared among the recorded neurons consistently across sessions. Limiting to 2 dimensions could result in inconsistent identification of the latent dimensions across sessions, thereby limiting alignment quality.

Some applications may require only a subset of dimensions. For instance, previous studies on working memory suggest that specific latent dimensions stably encode memory states, even though overall neural activity continues to evolve dynamically (e.g., Murray et al., 2017). While five latent dimensions may optimally capture overall neural population activity, certain brain states such as working memory states may primarily rely on just one or two specific dimensions. In these cases, we may want to focus on those relevant dimensions to affect the brain state. We will revise our paper to include these points in the main text.
> 9. Consistent terminology...

Agreed about consistent terminology. For the stimulation-response model, we will define the stimulation-response model in the introduction and consistently use it throughout the paper. 
For the use of pre-stimulation and pre-uStim, we used pre-uStim when referring specifically to electrical microstimulation, and pre-stimulation when including other types of stimulation (e.g., optogenetics).
> 10. There is no Fig. 2C...

Thanks, we will update it to Fig. 2B.
> 11. MiSO also performs...

We summarize the differences between OMiSO and MiSO below, which we will bring out more clearly in our paper.

1. MiSO does not consider the brain state when predicting the brain’s response to stimulation. In contrast, OMiSO explicitly models the brain state, allowing it to capture trial-to-trial differences in pre-stimulation brain state. This results in more precise prediction and control of neural population activity.
2. MiSO uses a tabular approach that stores the predicted post-stimulation state for each candidate stimulation pattern and updates only the entry corresponding to the tested pattern. This approach is sample inefficient as it does not propagate what can be learned from a new observation across patterns. OMiSO leverages an inverse model and updates its parameters online, enabling learning beyond the tested stimulation pattern. Consequently, OMiSO learns more efficiently and can adapt quickly with fewer observations.
3. The tabular method in MiSO becomes impractical as the stimulation parameter space grows, due to the increase in table size. OMiSO’s model-based approach scales more effectively to richer parameter spaces. This scalability allowed us to extend uStim parameter space to the 5-electrode uStim, compared to the 2-electrode uStim explored in MiSO.

We will update the paper to clarify these innovations. While OMiSO introduces multiple innovations, we chose to highlight the online model component in its name, as it played the most critical role in both incorporating brain state information and scaling the method to richer stimulation spaces.
> Originality: While there...

The reviewer raises a great point. We will update the paper to clarify that, while previous deep brain stimulation (DBS) studies have focused on manipulating low-dimensional biomarkers such as LFPs, our work introduces a novel approach to manipulate low-dimensional representations of multi-dimensional neural population activity. Although both approaches operate in low-dimensional spaces, our method makes a significant advancement because compared to LFPs, spiking activity tends to be less spatially correlated across nearby electrodes and can capture more detailed information about underlying neural computations. This enables us to achieve more precise control of neural population activity.

Our choice to focus on the low-d representation of neural population activity is motivated by many recent studies showing that the essential changes in neural activity underlying sensory, cognitive, and motor processes can be captured by low-d spaces (see Cunningham & Yu 2014, Saxena & Cunningham 2019, Ebitz & Hayden 2021). Furthermore, in brain-computer interfaces, it is possible to accurately decode movement intent from low-d representations of population activity (e.g., Degenhart et al., 2020). These insights inspired the design of OMiSO to operate within a low-d space.  While we show OMiSO can shape neural activity within the latent space, future work can test whether doing so produces meaningful changes in behavior. The success in this direction could be a major step forward for both clinical and scientific applications. 
> That using PPO...

One way to incorporate pre-stimulation neural states in MiSO is by discretization. For example, we could divide the latent neural activity state along each latent dimension into five discrete bins. This approach may work when the latent dimensionality is small. However, it becomes quickly infeasible as the dimensionality increases. For instance, with 15,504 stimulation patterns and a 5-d latent space discretized into 5 bins per dimension, we would need to optimize a table with 387,600 entries (15,504x5×5). Optimizing such a large table with only a few hundred experimental trials is extremely challenging. In contrast, OMiSO can efficiently handle continuous pre-stimulation latent states, offering a more scalable method.

Thank you to the reviewer for the constructive comments. Our responses are in the text below:

> 1. My primary concern is that reinforcement learning terminology seems to be used very loosely here. While that doesn't overshadow the main contributions of the paper, this being a machine learning venue does require either further explaining or rewriting. …..I am completely fine with the authors saying that they update the model using a PPO-inspired loss function so that the inverse model doesn't deviate much between consecutive trials. Alternatively, I would like a concrete definition of the RL problem if the authors want to stick to referring to these approaches as behavior cloning and PPO.

We appreciate the reviewer highlighting this point. While the design of OMiSO was inspired by RL, we agree that RL terminology was used loosely in the writing. In the revision, we will explain OMiSO without relying on RL concepts. Specifically, we will describe the "behavioral cloning" component as a supervised learning problem trained on synthetic data, as suggested by the reviewer. For the online update procedure, we will refer to the objective as a PPO-inspired loss function, as the reviewer suggests. These edits should provide a more accurate description of the method while avoiding confusion related to RL terminology.

> 2. Some of the choices made during the algorithm are unclear from the main text / methodology, making it hard to fully wrap one's head around it. Crucially, after learning the forward model on low-dimensional projection of the data, the authors further select of those dimensions to learn the inverse model. The rationale behind this is unclear to me. Is this is a computational bottleneck? Presumably, factor analysis already compresses neural data to a low-dimensional space, is this further compression necessary as it presumably results in not being able to control certain neural dimensions?

In principle, OMiSO can operate by defining the target state in all $m$ dimensions of the latent space. However, there are two key reasons why users might prefer to define the target in a lower-dimensional subspace, as we did in our experiments.
 
Firstly, not all latent dimensions are equally suitable for reliable perturbation of neural activity. For example, some dimensions may be aligned poorly across sessions because they are not consistently present in every session, while others may not be directly modifiable by stimulation. Thus, in our work, to evaluate the optimization performance of OMiSO, we selected target latent dimensions satisfying two conditions: 1) they are well-aligned across multiple sessions, and 2) uStim can induce diverse latent activity states along these dimensions (Section S3, line 457). For 1), we computed the cosine similarity of each column vector of $\tilde{\Lambda_i}$ (eq. 3) between a reference session and all other training sessions, which quantifies the consistency of each aligned latent dimension across sessions. For 2), we visualized the post-uStim state (eq. 4) induced in each single trial during the training sessions to assess the diversity of the induced latent activity.

Secondly, some scientific or clinical applications may require only a subset of dimensions. Previous studies investigated output-potent and output-null dimensions in the latent space, where only certain dimensions directly influence behavior or downstream processes (e.g., Kaufman et al., 2014). For instance, previous studies on working memory suggest that specific latent dimensions stably encode memory states, even though overall neural activity continues to evolve dynamically (Murray et al., 2017; Parthasarathy et al., 2019; Soldado-Magraner et al., 2025). While five latent dimensions may optimally capture overall neural population activity, certain brain states such as working memory states may primarily rely on just one or two specific dimensions. In these cases, we may want to focus on those relevant dimensions to affect the brain state. 

We will revise our paper to include these points in the main text.

> 1. In the introduction, the authors don't make it clear what "brain state" means. Later on it is clear that the authors are referring to a low-d projection of neural activity, but through the introduction it is unclear whether this refers to a high-level cognitive state etc, and it would help the readers a lot to know this upfront.

Agreed, we will add a clarification that “brain state” refers to low-d projection of recorded neural population activity in this study.

> 2. Forward model: In line 118, what kind of function does represent? The supplement suggests these are deep networks, which would be helpful to clarify here.

In our animal experiments, we used a combination of a CNN and a RNN (Section S1) as the function $f$. We kept the description in the main text general (i.e., any function $f$) to emphasize the flexibility of our framework because the stimulation-response model architecture could, in principle, be any architecture depending on the application and data characteristics. However, we agree that specifying the architecture used in our experiments would improve clarity. We will revise the main text to explicitly state the architecture we used in this study.

> 1. While the paper improves upon MiSO, it inherits fundamental limitations—notably, the low-dimensional stimulation parameter space (constrained by dual-electrode setups) inherently restricts the spatial scope of neuromodulation. The work focuses on algorithmic refinements rather than addressing these hardware-imposed boundaries, leaving the core challenge unresolved.

A substantial advancement of this work over MiSO is that we move beyond the dual-electrode uStim setup. In this study, we applied uStim using up to 5 electrodes. In principle, our uStim device is capable of supporting much more flexible stimulation configurations, including arbitrary combinations of electrodes (up to the 96 available with our hardware), as well as different amplitude, frequency, and waveform choices. The main constraints on our stimulation parameter space stem from biological safety limits, specifically, the total current that can be safely delivered, rather than limitations imposed by hardware. We agree with the reviewer that future developments in stimulation hardware (e.g., devices that allow precise control of current return paths or significantly lower latency for reconfiguration) is another critical field to expand the capability of neuromodulation technology. We believe that OMiSO is well-suited to take advantage of such advances, as our framework is generalizable to a wide range of stimulation parameter spaces.

> 2. The chosen metrics (e.g., accuracy in reaching target states) may not fully capture the biological efficacy of neural control, especially given the dynamic nature of brain states.

We agree. To manipulate behavior or brain state, it may be important to create a sequence of neural activity evolving over time (i.e., a target neural trajectory), rather than achieving a single static target state because many of the brain's computations are believed to rely on particular time courses of neural activity (e.g., decision making). Taking into account the time courses of neural activity is precisely where we are heading next, and our ongoing goal is to extend OMiSO to account for the temporal dynamics of brain activity. This could be achieved, for instance, by incorporating a dynamical model of the brain that predicts how neural activity will evolve over time. The prediction from this model guides the stimulation pattern selection process by suggesting what neural activity state to achieve at each time point to achieve a desired evolution over time.

> 3. Due to inter-session variability in neural activity, the claimed optimization benefits require validation across totally unseen sessions/timepoints to demonstrate robustness. The authors should discuss strategies to mitigate session-dependent confounds.

We agree that to demonstrate robustness, we need strategies to mitigate session-dependent confounds to generalize to a new session. This is particularly important in neuroscience applications, where the recorded neural activity can be non-stationary across days due to small movements of the recording electrodes relative to the brain and changes in the neural circuits.  As a result, a model that performs well in one session may fail in another. Stimulation frameworks need to be able to overcome this variability. To address this challenge and demonstrate the robustness of OMiSO, we designed our experiments and analyses in the following ways:

1. We trained the stimulation-response model using all but one experimental session and evaluated it on the held-out session (Fig. 2B, Section S6). This ensured that the model was evaluated on a totally unseen session.
2. We trained an inverse model using data from training sessions and tested its performance in totally unseen sessions (Fig. 3D, Section S6).
3. We tested the robustness of OMiSO by running adaptive stimulation optimization in totally unseen sessions not used during the inverse model training (Fig. 4E, Section S6).

In all these evaluations, we ensured that the test sessions were entirely held out from training. The consistent performance across these unseen sessions provided strong evidence that OMiSO can generalize across sessions and is robust to inter-session variability.

1. Add a mathematical problem statement to Section 2.1 to clearly frame the overall objective in machine learning terms:

Given a target brain state $z^{Targ}$, find a stimulation configuration $s$ that induces a brain state $z_s$ minimizing the error to the target:
$$
\underset{s}{\operatorname{argmin}} ||z^{Targ}-z_s||_1 \\
$$

2. Incorporate the notation introduced in the problem statement in Fig. 1 to clarify how the machine learning formulation maps to our specific neuroscience application.
　
> 2. Limited novelty: Core components (Factor Analysis, behavior cloning, PPO) are not new and their integration is not clearly justified as novel.

Our contribution lies in the novel integration of these components and demonstrating that this combination is effective for neuroscience applications. Designing a framework that works reliably in neuroscience settings is non-trivial. It requires addressing domain-specific challenges such as inter-trial and inter-session neural variability (due to shifting brain state over time, recording instabilities, and changes in neural circuits), a limited number of neural recording samples, and interfacing with neural recording and stimulation devices in real time. Each component of OMiSO was selected after extensive experimentation to satisfy these constraints. FA was chosen based on its success in BCI applications by stably representing neural population activity across sessions. BC and PPO were selected for their robustness under real-time adaptive stimulation experiments even with a limited number of observations. While the individual components are not novel, our contribution is in the careful integration of them to satisfy the unique requirements in neuroscience applications.
　　
> 1. In Section 2.2, you mention that due to the large stimulation parameter space, only a small subset of possible patterns can be tested within a session. To address this, OMiSO first identifies a low-dimensional latent space of the high-dimensional neural population activity. Given this, could you clarify why you chose to model the latent space from spiking activity rather than directly leveraging low-dimensional biomarkers such as local field potentials (LFPs), which are commonly used in clinical settings? Additionally, do you have any experimental comparisons showing that OMiSO outperforms LFP-based stimulation methods?

Our current work focuses on spiking activity because it provides richer and higher-resolution neural signals than LFPs. Compared to LFPs, spiking activity tends to be less spatially correlated across nearby electrodes and can capture more detailed information about underlying neural computations (Kajikawa et al., 2011).

At the same time, we agree that LFPs are highly relevant, especially in clinical settings. While our current experiments focus on spiking data, the OMiSO framework is generalizable and could be applied to control LFP activity as well. Specifically, one could train a stimulation-response model to predict evoked LFPs from different stimulation patterns, and then use the same behavior cloning and PPO-based online update strategy to perform adaptive stimulation experiments.
　　
> 2. Could you elaborate on the key technical and application-level differences between OMiSO and previous methods such as MiSO? A clear comparison would help readers better understand the novelty and specific contributions of your approach.

We summarize here the key technical and application-level differences between OMiSO and MiSO below, which we will bring out more clearly in our paper.

**Technical differences**:
1. *Incorporation of brain state*: MiSO does not consider the brain state when predicting the brain’s response to stimulation. In contrast, OMiSO explicitly models the brain state, allowing it to capture trial-to-trial differences in pre-stimulation brain state. This results in more precise prediction and control of neural population activity.
2. *Sample efficient online model*: MiSO uses a tabular approach that stores the predicted post-stimulation state for each candidate stimulation pattern and updates only the entry corresponding to the tested pattern. This approach is sample inefficient as it does not propagate what can be learned from a new observation across patterns. OMiSO leverages an inverse model and updates its parameters online, enabling learning beyond the tested stimulation pattern. Consequently, OMiSO learns more efficiently and can adapt quickly with fewer observations.
3. *Scalability*: The tabular method in MiSO becomes impractical as the stimulation parameter space grows, due to the increase in table size. OMiSO’s model-based approach scales more effectively to richer parameter spaces. This scalability allowed us to extend stimulation parameter space to the 5-electrode stimulation, compared to the 2-electrode stimulation explored in MiSO.

**Application-level differences**:
1. *Dependency on the brain state*: In applications which use strong stimulation (e.g., large currents), the brain responses to stimulation might not depend on the pre-stimulation brain state (e.g., all the neurons are excited or suppressed). In such cases, MiSO may be sufficient. However, when stimulation is used to modulate neural activity, which is likely needed in most applications, the brain’s response to stimulation will depend on the pre-stimulation brain state, as shown in Fig. 2. In this case, OMiSO would work better than MiSO.
2. *Experimental session duration*: If the experimental session is short (e.g., a few minutes) and the brain state remains stable throughout, MiSO may be sufficient. On the other hand, if the experimental session is longer than a few minutes (likely for most applications) and there are shifts in brain state, OMiSO may be necessary to compensate for the shift.
3. *Computation speed requirements*: For applications that require selecting a stimulation pattern within a very short time window, MiSO may be a good choice. However, if longer computation times are acceptable or a fast GPU infrastructure is available, OMiSO can provide more precise control of neural population activity.

> 3. I would appreciate clarification on the connection between your monkey experiments and clinical deep brain stimulation (DBS). My understanding is that DBS is typically used in disease treatment contexts (e.g., Parkinson’s disease). How does your framework relate to that setting? Specifically, is the goal of OMiSO to generalize toward clinical applications, or is it primarily intended as a neuroscience tool for experimental control (e.g., guiding the monkey to desired neural states)?

Our goal includes both clinical and neuroscience research applications. We designed OMiSO as a framework that can be adapted to both contexts by modifying the target brain state and by defining the appropriateness of a given stimulation pattern for achieving the target state (eq. 7).
 
In clinical DBS applications, for example, the target could be defined as a healthy brain state. OMiSO can then identify stimulation patterns that move neural activity towards this desired state. OMiSO could also be used to stay away from unhealthy brain states by maximizing the distance from unhealthy brain states.

In neuroscience research applications, OMiSO can be used as a tool for different stimulation modalities (electrical microstimulation, optogenetic stimulation, etc) to study sensory, cognitive, and motor function. For instance, researchers can perturb neural activity away from one working memory state to another working memory state to investigate how the neural population activity evolves after such perturbation.

OMiSO does not use a model of the environment (i.e., the brain), and thus, it is not a model-based reinforcement learning approach. However, this is a great point, and we are working on extending OMiSO toward a model-based reinforcement learning framework. The current version of OMiSO focuses on a single time-step stimulation to achieve a target brain state at a single time point. However, many behaviors and brain states involve neural activity evolving over time. Thus, extending OMiSO to control neural population activity over time may be an important direction to affect such behaviors or brain states. Such an extension requires a model that incorporates stimulation inputs and predicts future brain states, thereby guiding the selection of stimulation patterns over multiple time steps.

summary.value: This paper introduces Online MicroStimulation Optimization (OMiSO), a closed-loop brain stimulation framework designed to modulate neural population activity more precisely by leveraging the brain’s ongoing state. Unlike prior methods, OMiSO conditions stimulation parameter selection on pre-stimulation neural activity and continuously adapts its model based on observed responses. The framework builds a stimulation-response model online and inverts it to choose stimulation parameters that drive neural activity toward specified target states. The approach was validated in a non-human primate experiment using intracortical microstimulation, where it outperformed baseline methods lacking brain state awareness or adaptive learning. While the method shows strong empirical results and is broadly applicable to different stimulation modalities, its effectiveness may vary depending on the stability of neural dynamics and consistency between training and deployment conditions. Overall, OMiSO presents a principled and flexible framework that enhances the precision of neural control, with promising implications for both neuroscience research and clinical neuromodulation.

summary.value:
The authors introduce an algorithm to identify desired stimulations in order to move brain activity to a target state, in a closed loop. 
The key ingredients involve learning an inverse mapping that outputs the desired stimulation pattern required to reach a target state from the previous state of neural activity, and then updating this mapping online as more data is collected during the experiment. They show that taking into account the current state of the brain in this pipeline results in far better performance in terms of reaching the target state relative to existing methods such as MiSo. In particular, results from stimulations in macaque PFC recordings using Utah array show successful reaching of target state in a low-dimensional space.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

1. The paper is well-written, key claims and results are easily to follow.
2. It attempts to solve an impactful and translatable problem, and is extremely significant to research at the cross roads of machine learning and neuroscience. 
3. The methodology overall makes sense, the high-level pipeline is novel, and the experiments are thoroughly done on real macaques.
4.  I also appreciate the supplement discussion re how the online updates are done without hindering the generation of stimulation patterns themselves. 

Weaknesses:
1. My primary concern is that reinforcement learning terminology seems to be used very loosely here. While that doesn't overshadow the main contributions of the paper, this being a machine learning venue does require either further explaining or rewriting. For example, the inverse model training is really  a supervised problem on synthetic data generated from the forward model. Calling it behavior cloning is confusing in my opinion, because it is unclear what the markov decision process looks like here. In its current form "state" in the MDP sense includes past + current ($z_{pre}$) and future ($z_{post}$) information. If we think of the action as the stimulation, what should the next markovian state look like? Is there a sequential problem underlying this process at all that I might be missing? Relatedly, PPO also seems to be loosely used, where the advantage function typically is defined as $A(s,a) = Q(s,a)-V(s)$. I am completely fine with the authors saying that they update the model using a PPO-inspired loss function so that the inverse model doesn't deviate much between consecutive trials. Alternatively, I would like a concrete definition of the RL problem if the authors wants to stick to referring to these approaches as behavior cloning and PPO. 

2. Some of the choices made during the algorithm are unclear from the main text / methodology, making it hard to fully wrap one's head around it. Crucially, after learning the forward model on low-dimensional projection of the data, the authors further select $l$ of those dimensions to learn the inverse model. The rationale behind this is unclear to me. Is this is a computational bottleneck? Presumably, factor analysis already compresses neural data to a low-dimensional space, is this further compression necessary as it presumably results in not being able to control certain neural dimensions?

questions.value:
Aside from some of my questions listed in the weakness section, I have the following questions / comments:

1. In the introduction, the authors don't make it clear what "brain state" means. Later on it is clear that the authors are referring to a low-d projection of neural activity, but through the introduction it is unclear whether this refers to a high-level cognitive state etc, and it would help the readers a lot to know this upfront.

2. Forward model: In line 118, what kind of function does $f$ represent? The supplement suggests these are deep networks, which would be helpful to clarify here.

3. What if a reaching a target brain state requires multiple steps of stimulations? How would this algorithm handle such a case given intermediate target states may be unknown in that setting?

Minor comments / typos:
1. Lines 36-39: this sentence needs to be broken into two for readability.
2. Line 83: I am assuming this should be $e^i \in \\{1,...n_i\\}$.

summary.value: The authors developed a method called OMiSO, which, given the current neural population state and the desired state, outputs an optimal stimulation pattern that will move the state to the desired state. In this study, the authors focus on not the full neural state space, but the low-dimensional latent state obtained from factor analysis. Factor analysis is performed for each session, and the latent spaces are aligned, following the same approach as in MiSO. The authors then fit a stimulation-response model that predicts the latent state after stimulation, given the latent state before stimulation and the stimulation pattern. This model is then used to generate enough data to fit an RL model via behavioral cloning. The RL model’s job is to predict, given the pre-stimulation latent state and the target latent state, what the stimulus pattern should be. After these steps, which are so far done offline, the authors further refine the RL model online via PPO as new data comes in. The authors test their method on a real monkey electrophysiology dataset and find superior performance compared to baselines and a recent method, MiSO.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Quality**: The authors’ claims are well supported by experiments. 

1. The authors claim that leveraging pre-stimulation neural activity for predicting optimal stimulation patterns can be helpful, and show experimental evidence that the latent states of the monkey before and after stimulation for two different stimuli are distinguishable. I agree that providing the model with the pre-stimulation activity (more data) is helpful, and wonder if, for their setup, providing it with experimental stimuli (the location of the target dots) can make it even better. What do the authors think about including “optional data” (e.g., target location in this case, but could be some other data in general) as one of the features of the model?

2. The authors show evidence that their stimulation-response model works well, by experimenting with different neural network architectures. The authors report the hyperparameters in the Supplementary Material. The authors also justify their stimulation-response inverse model by comparing it to a “perfect” inversion model, which constructs a table of all possible combinations of stimulation patterns and their corresponding states post-stimulation. This perfect inversion model predicts the optimal stimulation patterns from the post-stimulation states using this table (a table including pre-stimulation combinations may be infeasible due to the latent space being continuous and large). Their inverse model (trained by BC) performs well compared to the perfect inversion model.

3. Lastly, the authors show evidence that refining their predictions online via PPO helps in actual brain stimulation experiments. 14 sessions were used to make comparisons between MiSO, OMiSO, and their perfect inversion model without pre-stimulation states. The authors show that OMiSO performs better than the baseline methods in this experiment.


**Clarity**: The work is overall clear and well-organized. There were a few places where I thought would benefit from clarification.

1. Equations (1-4) are exactly the same as Equations (1-4) of the MiSO paper, and as far as I understand, there is no conceptual difference between the latent alignment procedure performed by MiSO and that performed in this work. I think the authors could instead cite MiSO for this Section, with just Eq. 4 in the paper, as this one is used throughout the later Sections.

2. It wasn’t clear from the main text how the function f (the stimulation-response model) was modeled when it was first introduced in L118. Adding a sentence early on that the network architectures in Fig. 2B are used for their function f, and that the specific architectures are shown in Fig. S1, could be helpful. This is also true for \phi_\theta, first introduced in L128. Perhaps mentioning that this is an MLP early on could be helpful.

3. It wasn’t clear in the beginning why Z is a matrix with t, whereas z is a vector without t? If I understand correctly, this is because for Z, the stimulation-response model f can use 1 to 5 pre-uStim time bins. I think this information could be added early on to make it clearer.

4. The authors mention that “OMiSO performs R-fold cross validation where every session is used as a validation set once (see Section S4)”. S4 didn’t specify this, and perhaps mentioning S6 in S4 makes sense.

5. It wasn’t clear from the main text how the experiments were run -- for each trial, how did they choose which method to use? For Fig. 4D, the authors show the average predicted post-stimulation state and target state, along with single-trial predictions of post-stimulation states. Is the plot in Fig. 4E made by first taking the Euclidean distance between the average predicted state and the target state for each session, and then computing the mean and standard error across the 14 sessions? For L312, should this be p=0.05 and p=0.01, and not p<0.05 and p<0.01?

6. L157: The number of stimulus patterns is not in real space but in integer space.

7. L195: What does it mean for the baseline b to be used “to evaluate the induced post-uStim activity”? How does this baseline b help here?

8. After doing dimensionality reduction to m=5 dimensions, how does the user select l from m? How m and l were selected was not explained in S3 but in S1 (only for m). If l components are selected from m, I think the same state in this l-dimensional latent space doesn’t represent the same space in neural space or the m-dimensional latent space. Would results be different if the authors used l=m=5, or l=m=2? I think a justification for subselection would be helpful. How does increasing or decreasing l or m affect model performance (both accuracy and speed)? 

9. Consistent terminology could help: for example, sometimes the stimulation-response model is referred to as the statistical model, and pre-uStim is referred to as pre-stimulation.

10. There is no Fig. 2C (L268).

11. MiSO also performs online inference, but this method is called Online MiSO. Is the online-ness the most important factor that distinguishes between this approach and MiSO? A few sentences discussing in-depth how this approach differs from MiSO would be helpful.

**Significance**: Optimal online control of the neural population state from one state to another is a key challenge in BCI, and OMiSO suggests a new approach to solve this problem. The authors apply their method to real brain stimulation experiments in monkeys and demonstrate its efficacy in comparison to a previous method, MiSO. Their demonstration of their method and baselines in actual experimental settings is a big strength of this paper. The method also consists of modular steps, and each step of the method can be replaced without affecting the other steps. For example, in the paper, factor analysis and the latent alignment method via Procrustes optimization were used in one of the steps, and this may be replaced by other fast dimensionality reduction methods and alignment methods in the future if one finds improvement over the current one. This modularity allows accessing each step of the model and what features most affect its performance.

**Originality**: While there is previous work incorporating pre-stimulation neural state for choosing optimal stimulation patterns, the authors suggest that this is the first to incorporate pre-stimulation activity for manipulating high-dimensional neural population state. Because this work focuses on the prediction of the low-dimensional latent state, I think it would help to show prediction in the neural population state (i.e., predictions on firing rates of individual neurons) are close to the observed high-dimensional neural population state. Currently, the authors focus on the learned low-dimensional state, and it is not clear whether the learned low-dimensional state accurately captures the high-dimensional neural population state. As mentioned in Clarity point 8 above, it may also be the case that if the users subselect arbitrary dimensions in the m-dimensional latent space, it would be hard to recover the full high-dimensional neural population state. A discussion on how this can be addressed would be helpful. That using PPO to update/refine the predictions in real-time is better than the method used in MiSO is also an interesting finding. summary.value: This paper introduces OMiSO (Online MicroStimulation Optimization), a brain stimulation framework that optimizes stimulation parameters by explicitly modeling the pre-stimulation neural state to achieve precise control over population-level neural activity. This work proposes a closed-loop, state-aware optimization approach, which dynamically adapts stimulation protocols based on real-time neural recordings.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. The framework introduces optimal parameter selection conditioned on pre-stimulation brain states—a well-established control-theoretic principle previously unrealized in MiSO systems. This enables context-aware stimulation tailored to baseline neural activity.

2. By continuously refining parameters using newly observed stimulation responses, OMiSO overcomes the limitation of MiSO's restricted parameter-space search. The proposed reinforcement learning algorithm dynamically optimizes stimulation protocols, achieving superior neural control.

Weaknesses:
1. While the paper improves upon MiSO, it inherits fundamental limitations—notably, the low-dimensional stimulation parameter space (constrained by dual-electrode setups) inherently restricts the spatial scope of neuromodulation. The work focuses on algorithmic refinements rather than addressing these hardware-imposed boundaries, leaving the core challenge unresolved.

2. The chosen metrics (e.g., accuracy in reaching target states) may not fully capture the biological efficacy of neural control, especially given the dynamic nature of brain states.

3. Due to inter-session variability in neural activity, the claimed optimization benefits require validation across totally unseen sessions/timepoints to demonstrate robustness. The authors should discuss strategies to mitigate session-dependent confounds.

title.value: OMiSO: Adaptive optimization of state-dependent brain stimulation to shape neural population states

TLDR.value: OMiSO (Online MicroStimulation Optimization): a brain stimulation framework to drive neural population activity toward specified states by adaptively choosing stimulation parameters based on brain state information

abstract.value: The coordinated activity of neural populations underlies myriad brain functions. Manipulating this activity using brain stimulation techniques has great potential for scientific and clinical applications, as they causally influence the nervous system. To improve the accuracy by which one can manipulate neural activity, it is important to (1) take into account the pre-stimulation brain state, which can influence the brain’s response to stimulation, and (2) adaptively update stimulation parameters over time to compensate for changes in the brain’s response to stimulation. In this work, we propose Online MicroStimulation Optimization (OMiSO), a brain stimulation framework that leverages brain state information to find stimulation parameters that can drive neural population activity toward specified states. OMiSO includes two key advances: i) training a stimulation-response model that leverages the pre-stimulation brain state, and inverting this model to choose the stimulation parameters, and ii) updating this inverse model online using newly-observed responses to stimulation. We tested OMiSO using intracortical microstimulation with a ``Utah'' array and found that it outperformed competing methods that do not incorporate these advances. Taken together, OMiSO provides greater accuracy in achieving specified activity states, thereby advancing neuromodulation technologies for understanding the brain and for treating brain disorders.
